Django Introduction.exp: Introduction to Django and its ecosystem.

What is Django: Django is a high-level Python web framework that encourages rapid development with a clean, pragmatic design. It follows the 'batteries-included' philosophy, providing ORM, admin panel, authentication, forms, templates, and more out of the box. Django uses the MTV (Model-Template-View) architectural pattern, which is similar to MVC but with different naming. It emphasizes DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and security by default.

# Install Django
pip install django

# Create a project
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite

# Run development server
python manage.py runserver

# Create an app
python manage.py startapp blog

# Project structure:
# mysite/
#   manage.py
#   mysite/
#     settings.py
#     urls.py
#     wsgi.py
#   blog/

Project Structure: A Django project consists of a project directory and one or more apps. The project contains settings, root URL configuration, and WSGI/ASGI configuration. Apps are reusable modules that contain models, views, templates, and static files. The manage.py script is a command-line utility for administrative tasks. key files: settings.py (configuration), urls.py (URL routing), wsgi.py (deployment entry), asgi.py (async deployment entry). Each app has its own migrations, admin, tests, and apps configuration.

mysite/

├── mysite/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py   # Database, apps, middleware, templates
│   ├── urls.py       # Root URL configuration
│   ├── asgi.py       # Async server entry
│   └── wsgi.py       # WSGI server entry

Settings & Configuration: Django settings control every aspect of the framework. Key settings: INSTALLED_APPS (list of enabled apps), MIDDLEWARE (request/response processing pipeline), DATABASES (database configuration), TEMPLATES (template engine config), STATIC_URL/STATIC_ROOT (static files), MEDIA_URL/MEDIA_ROOT (user uploads). Use python-decouple or django-environ for environment variables. SECRET_KEY must be kept secret. DEBUG=False in production. ALLOWED_HOSTS restricts domain names.

Django Data.exp: Working with data and APIs in Django.

Testing in Django: Django's test framework extends Python's unittest. Use TestCase for database-backed tests. Client simulates browser requests. Factory Boy creates test data. pytest-django is a popular alternative. Key assertions: assertEqual, assertContains, assertTemplateUsed, assertRedirects, assertQuerysetEqual. Tests live in tests.py per app or a tests/ directory. Run with python manage.py test. Use --keepdb to preserve test database between runs.

Defining Models: Models are Python classes that define the structure of your database tables. Each model maps to a single database table, and each attribute maps to a database column. Django automatically creates the table schema, manages relationships (ForeignKey, ManyToManyField, OneToOneField), and provides a powerful QuerySet API. Common field types: CharField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, DateTimeField, TextField, EmailField, URLField, FileField, ImageField. Field options: null, blank, default, unique, choices, verbose_name, help_text.

from django.db import models
from django.utils import timezone

class Category(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    description = models.TextField(blank=True)

    class Meta:
        verbose_name_plural = 'categories'
        ordering = ['name']

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    author = models.ForeignKey(
        'auth.User', on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='blog_posts'
    )
    category = models.ForeignKey(
        Category, on_delete=models.SET_NULL,
        null=True, related_name='posts'
    )
    tags = models.ManyToManyField('Tag', blank=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title
Migrations: Migrations are Django's way of propagating model changes to the database schema. They're Python files that describe database operations. Key commands: makemigrations (creates migration files), migrate (applies migrations), sqlmigrate (shows SQL), showmigrations (lists migrations). Migrations track dependencies and can be merged. Always create migrations after changing models. Use --name for custom migration names. For data migrations, create empty migration and use RunPython.

# Terminal commands
python manage.py makemigrations          # Create migrations
python manage.py migrate                  # Apply migrations
python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0001     # View SQL
python manage.py showmigrations           # List all migrations

# After changing a model, always run:
# python manage.py makemigrations <app_name>
# python manage.py migrate

# Data migration example:
# python manage.py makemigrations <app> --empty

# Generated file: blog/migrations/0002_populate_slugs.py
from django.db import migrations

def populate_slugs(apps, schema_editor):
    Post = apps.get_model('blog', 'Post')
    for post in Post.objects.all():
        post.slug = post.title.lower().replace(' ', '-')
        post.save()

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [
        ('blog', '0001_initial'),
    ]
    operations = [
        migrations.RunPython(populate_slugs),
    ]
QuerySet API: QuerySets are lazy database lookups that allow chaining filters. They are evaluated only when iterated, sliced, or converted to list. Key methods: all(), filter(), exclude(), get(), create(), update(), delete(), order_by(), values(), values_list(), select_related(), prefetch_related(), annotate(), aggregate(), distinct(), count(), exists(), first(), last(), latest(), earliest(). Field lookups: exact, iexact, contains, icontains, in, gt, gte, lt, lte, startswith, endswith, range, date, year, month, day, isnull, regex, iregex.

from django.db.models import Count, Q
from blog.models import Post

# Basic queries
posts = Post.objects.all()
posts = Post.objects.filter(published=True)
posts = Post.objects.exclude(category=None)

# Chaining
posts = Post.objects.filter(
    published=True
).select_related('author').order_by('-created')

# Complex filters with Q
posts = Post.objects.filter(
    Q(title__icontains='django') |
    Q(body__icontains='django')
)

# Aggregation
from django.db.models import Count, Avg
stats = Post.objects.aggregate(
    total=Count('id'),
    avg_comments=Avg('comment_count')
)

# Annotation
categories = Category.objects.annotate(
    post_count=Count('posts')
).filter(post_count__gt=0)

# Related objects
post = Post.objects.get(id=1)
comments = post.comment_set.all()  # reverse relation

# Update
Post.objects.filter(published=False).update(published=True)

# Defer / Only (performance)
Post.objects.defer('body').all()
Post.objects.only('title', 'created')
Relationships: Django supports three relationship types: ForeignKey (many-to-one), ManyToManyField (many-to-many), and OneToOneField (one-to-one). ForeignKey requires on_delete option (CASCADE, PROTECT, SET_NULL, SET_DEFAULT, SET(), DO_NOTHING, RESTRICT). related_name defines reverse relation name (default: modelname_set). ManyToManyField can use through for intermediary models with extra fields. OneToOneField extends another model (like inheritance). Generic Foreign Keys allow relations to any model.

from django.db import models
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

# One-to-Many (ForeignKey)
class Comment(models.Model):
    post = models.ForeignKey(
        'Post', on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='comments'
    )
    author = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    body = models.TextField()
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

# Many-to-Many with through table
class Membership(models.Model):
    person = models.ForeignKey('Person', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    group = models.ForeignKey('Group', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    date_joined = models.DateField(auto_now_add=True)
    invite_reason = models.CharField(max_length=64)

class Group(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=128)
    members = models.ManyToManyField(
        'Person', through='Membership'
    )

# One-to-One
class Profile(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(
        User, on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='profile'
    )
    bio = models.TextField(blank=True)
    avatar = models.ImageField(upload_to='avatars/')

# Usage
user = User.objects.get(id=1)
user.profile.bio  # OneToOne reverse
user.blog_posts.all()  # ForeignKey reverse
post.comments.all()  # ForeignKey reverse (related_name)

Function-Based Views: Function-based views (FBVs) are simple Python functions that take an HttpRequest and return an HttpResponse. They are the most straightforward way to handle requests. The function receives the request object and optional URL parameters. Returns HttpResponse, render(), redirect(), or JsonResponse. Can be decorated with @login_required, @require_http_methods, @csrf_exempt, etc. Simple and explicit but can become repetitive for CRUD operations.
Class-Based Views: Class-based views (CBVs) organize view logic into reusable classes. Django provides generic CBVs: ListView, DetailView, CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView, FormView, TemplateView, RedirectView. CBVs use attributes and methods for configuration: model, template_name, context_object_name, form_class, success_url, paginate_by. Override methods: get_queryset(), get_context_data(), form_valid(), get_success_url(). Mixins allow combining reusable behavior. CBVs reduce boilerplate for CRUD but have a steeper learning curve.
URL Configuration: URL configuration maps URL patterns to views using django.urls.path() and re_path(). Each URL pattern has a route, view, optional kwargs, and a unique name. Include() allows nesting app URL configs. path converters: str, int, slug, uuid, path. Custom path converters can be defined. Use namespacing with app_name and include with namespace. The {% url %} template tag reverses URL names. For complex patterns, use re_path() with regex. Always name your URLs for maintainability.

# mysite/urls.py (root)
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include
from django.conf import settings
from django.conf.urls.static import static

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('blog.urls')),
    path('api/', include('api.urls')),
]

# Serve media files in development
if settings.DEBUG:
    urlpatterns += static(
        settings.MEDIA_URL,
        document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT
    )


# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'blog'

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.PostListView.as_view(), name='post_list'),
    path('<slug:slug>/', views.PostDetailView.as_view(), name='post_detail'),
    path('create/', views.PostCreateView.as_view(), name='post_create'),
    path('<slug:slug>/update/', views.PostUpdateView.as_view(), name='post_update'),
    path('<slug:slug>/delete/', views.PostDeleteView.as_view(), name='post_delete'),
]

Template Language: Django template language uses {{ variables }} and {% tags %}. Variables can be attributes, dictionary keys, or list indices. Filters transform variables: date, default, length, upper, lower, title, pluralize, slugify, truncatechars, safe, escape, join. Tags control logic: {% if %}, {% for %}, {% block %}, {% extends %}, {% include %}, {% url %}, {% load %}, {% static %}. Template inheritance with {% extends %} and {% block %} is the most powerful feature. Context processors make variables available in all templates.

Static Files: Static files (CSS, JS, images) are managed via django.contrib.staticfiles. In development, use runserver. In production, use collectstatic to gather files. Configure STATIC_URL, STATICFILES_DIRS (additional directories), STATIC_ROOT (production destination). Use {% load static %} and {% static 'path' %} in templates. For user uploads, use MEDIA_URL and MEDIA_ROOT with ImageField/FileField. Whitenoise is a popular package for serving static files in production.

# settings.py — static & media files import os STATIC_URL = '/static/' STATICFILES_DIRS = [ BASE_DIR / 'static', BASE_DIR / 'blog' / 'static', ] STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles' MEDIA_URL = '/media/' MEDIA_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'media' {% load static %} # Production deployment # python manage.py collectstatic # This gathers all static files into STATIC_ROOT # With Whitenoise (production): MIDDLEWARE.insert(1, 'whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware') STORAGES = { 'staticfiles': { 'BACKEND': 'whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage', }, }

Django Forms: Django forms handle HTML form generation, validation, and processing. Form classes define fields with validation rules. Forms can be bound (with data) or unbound. Common fields: CharField, EmailField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, ChoiceField, MultipleChoiceField, FileField, ImageField. Validators: built-in (required, min_length, max_length, min_value, max_value), regex, custom. Widgets control HTML rendering: TextInput, Textarea, Select, CheckboxInput, RadioSelect, FileInput. Form rendering: form.as_p, form.as_table, form.as_ul, or manual field-by-field.
Form Processing: Form processing follows a pattern: GET renders empty form, POST validates and processes. Check request.method, instantiate form with request.POST (and request.FILES for uploads), call form.is_valid(), access cleaned_data, redirect on success or re-render with errors. ModelForm.save() creates or updates a model instance. Use commit=False for pre-save processing. FormSets manage multiple forms of the same type. Inline form sets handle related model forms.

User Authentication: Django's built-in authentication system handles users, groups, permissions, and sessions. The User model provides username, password, email, first_name, last_name. Extend via OneToOneField (Profile model) or AbstractUser (custom user model). Key views: LoginView, LogoutView, PasswordChangeView, PasswordResetView. Decorators: @login_required, @permission_required, @user_passes_test. Mixins: LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin. django.contrib.auth.urls provides all auth URL patterns.

# settings.py LOGIN_URL = '/accounts/login/' LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/' LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = '/' # mysite/urls.py urlpatterns += [ path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')), ] # Provides these URLs automatically: # accounts/login/ [name='login'] # accounts/logout/ [name='logout'] # accounts/password_change/ [name='password_change'] # accounts/password_reset/ [name='password_reset'] # In views from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin @login_required def profile_view(request): return render(request, 'profile.html', { 'user': request.user }) # Class-based class ProfileView(LoginRequiredMixin, TemplateView): template_name = 'profile.html' # In templates {% if user.is_authenticated %}

Permissions & Groups: Django's permission system assigns permissions to users and groups. Each model gets three default permissions: add_, change_, delete_, and optionally view_. Groups bundle permissions for role-based access. Check permissions with user.has_perm(), @permission_required, or PermissionRequiredMixin. Custom permissions can be defined in model Meta. The admin interface provides group and permission management. Object-level permissions require third-party packages like django-guardian.

from django.db import models from django.contrib.auth.models import User from django.contrib.auth.decorators import permission_required # Custom permission in model Meta class Article(models.Model): title = models.CharField(max_length=200) content = models.TextField() status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=[ ('draft', 'Draft'), ('published', 'Published'), ]) class Meta: permissions = [ ('can_publish', 'Can publish articles'), ('can_archive', 'Can archive articles'), ] # Checking permissions @permission_required('blog.can_publish') def publish_article(request, pk): article = Article.objects.get(pk=pk) article.status = 'published' article.save() return redirect('article_detail', pk=pk) # In templates {% if perms.blog.can_publish %} Publish {% endif %} # Programmatic user.has_perm('blog.can_publish') user.has_perms(['blog.add_article', 'blog.change_article']) # Groups from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, Permission editor_group, created = Group.objects.get_or_create(name='Editors') perm = Permission.objects.get(codename='can_publish') editor_group.permissions.add(perm) user.groups.add(editor_group)

Admin Customization: Django's admin interface provides automatic CRUD for models. Register models with admin.site.register() or use @admin.register() decorator. Customize with ModelAdmin options: list_display, list_filter, search_fields, list_editable, list_per_page, ordering, date_hierarchy, readonly_fields, fieldsets, exclude, inlines. Enhance with actions, custom templates, and widget overrides. Admin has built-in authentication, permissions, and history tracking.

DRF Basics: Django REST Framework (DRF) is a powerful toolkit for building Web APIs. Install with pip install djangorestframework. Core concepts: Serializers (convert complex types to/from JSON), Views (APIView, ViewSets), Routers (auto-generate URL patterns), Authentication & Permissions. DRF provides browsable API, content negotiation, throttling, filtering, and versioning. Use ModelSerializer for model-based serializers, ReadOnlyModelViewSet for read-only endpoints.
ViewSets & Routers: ViewSets combine logic for multiple actions (list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update, destroy) into a single class. ModelViewSet provides all CRUD operations. Routers automatically generate URL patterns from ViewSets. DefaultRouter creates API root view. Custom actions with @action decorator. Filter backends: DjangoFilterBackend, SearchFilter, OrderingFilter. Override get_queryset, perform_create, get_serializer_class for customization.

# views.py
from rest_framework import viewsets, filters, status
from rest_framework.decorators import action
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from django_filters.rest_framework import DjangoFilterBackend
from .models import Post, Comment
from .serializers import PostSerializer, CommentSerializer

class PostViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Post.objects.filter(published=True)
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
    lookup_field = 'slug'

    filter_backends = [
        DjangoFilterBackend,
        filters.SearchFilter,
        filters.OrderingFilter,
    ]
    filterset_fields = ['category__slug', 'author']
    search_fields = ['title', 'body']
    ordering_fields = ['created', 'title']

    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(author=self.request.user)

    @action(detail=True, methods=['post'],
            permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated])
    def comment(self, request, slug=None):
        post = self.get_object()
        serializer = CommentSerializer(data=request.data)
        if serializer.is_valid():
            serializer.save(post=post, author=request.user)
            return Response(serializer.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
        return Response(serializer.errors, status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)

    @action(detail=False)
    def recent(self, request):
        recent_posts = self.get_queryset()[:5]
        serializer = self.get_serializer(recent_posts, many=True)
        return Response(serializer.data)


# urls.py
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from .views import PostViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register(r'posts', PostViewSet, basename='post')

urlpatterns = router.urls

Production Deployment: Django deployment requires a production-ready web server (Gunicorn, uWSGI), reverse proxy (Nginx, Apache), and database (PostgreSQL). Environment variables for secrets. Use django-environ or python-decouple. Disable DEBUG, configure ALLOWED_HOSTS, use secure cookies, enable HTTPS. Static files served via Whitenoise or CDN. Media files served via Nginx or cloud storage (S3, GCS). Database connection pooling with pgbouncer. Caching with Redis/Memcached. Celery for async tasks. Sentry for error tracking.
